# Introduction

Why do policy actors do what they do? Why and how does a policy or a particular institutional arrangement change or remain immutable? Those are some of the most foundational questions in public policy research and practice. Several theoretical approaches and frameworks about the policy process have been developed to address them. For example, policy change has been explained through looking at changes in beliefs and coalitions [@sabatierPolicyChangeLearning1993], the shifting components of institutional arrangements over time [@ostromGoverningCommonsEvolution1990], the diffusion of policy ideas across political jurisdictions [@braunTakingGaltonProblem2006], the interplay of external events and institutional dynamics [@baumgartnerAgendasInstabilityAmerican1993], and the influence of policy entrepreneurs in coupling problems, solutions, and political conditions, [@kingdonAgendasAlternativesPublic1984], among others. 

The various policy process theories and frameworks have made significant contributions to the understanding of policymaking; however, we argue that policy learning plays a central role in policymaking that cuts across all of these approaches. Although definitions vary, policy learning can be understood as a process in which policy actors, acting within in particular political contexts and institutional settings, seek out and process information and knowledge about policy problems to update their understanding of the problems and viable solutions [@zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. The learning process produces a range of possible outcomes, including cognitive, such as updates in beliefs and preferences, whether confirmatory or transformative, as well as behavioral, such as changes in political advocacy strategies and other actions which may lead to different degrees of policy change [see @dunlopSystematisingPolicyLearning2013; @heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013; @plumerWhenDoesPolicy2024]. On this basis, policy learning can be as central to understanding the policy process by offering a coherent account of why policy actors and institutions behave as they do through tracing why, how, and when they learn about policy problems and viable solutions [see @kamkhajiPolicyLearningEuro2022; @zakiHelloDarknessMy2024]. In this view, learning is not merely something that occurs within policymaking, it is the foundation on which policymaking occurs. Therefore, explaining policy behavior and outcomes requires attending to the key attributes of learning, namely who learns, what they learn, from whom, how, and why. Put differently, we can better account for why policy actors behave in particular ways, and with what consequences, by treating their actions as a function of their learning processes [@dunlopSystematisingPolicyLearning2013; @zakiHelloDarknessMy2024].

The analytical potential of policy learning, together with its normative appeal, has spurred a flurry of research in which learning has evolved into a multifaceted concept that often resists universal definition. Accordingly, reviews of the policy learning literature document dozens of definitions of policy learning. These definitions are grounded in distinct ontological and epistemological assumptions and diverge in their analytical emphases, whether they privilege learning outcomes, the levels at which learning occurs, or the units of analysis, ranging from individuals to collectives, organizations, subsystems, and entire societies [@gerlakLearningOurWay2018; @zakiMeasuringPolicyLearning2024; @zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022].

The growth of policy learning has proceeded in several directions, including across the various theories and frameworks of policymaking. In the Multiple Streams Approach (MSA), recent work has shown how learning occurs within and across loosely coupled streams, for example through indicators, focusing events, and feedback that reshape problem definitions, through policy communities’ work on policy and instrument design, and through political learning and coupling practices in which entrepreneurs craft discursive links between problems, policies, and politics [@herwegMultipleStreamsFramework2023; @mockPolicyLearningFace2024; @blumMultipleStreamsFrameworkKnowledge2018]. Learning has also traveled into narrative and framing scholarship, most visibly in the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF), where narratives are treated as structured stories with characters and morals that actors deploy strategically; this makes narrative stability and change an empirically observable surface of belief dynamics and, increasingly, a basis for theorizing policy narrative learning as convergence on new narrative configurations over time [see @jonesNarrativePolicyFramework2010; @shanahanNarrativePolicyFramework2011; @bandelowNarrativesFramingPolicy2025; @jungSeekingHighGround2024]. Beyond MSF and NPF, learning is shown in policy diffusion and transfer models that formalize how governments learn from their own experiences and those of others’ [@voldenFormalModelLearning2008], in work spanning the policy cycle from design to implementation [@biegelbauerHowDifferentForms2016], as well as in classic accounts linking different learning dynamics to different orders of policy change, from incremental adjustments to paradigmatic shifts 
[@bennettLessonsLearningReconciling1992; @hallPolicyParadigmsSocial1993; @moysonCognitionPolicyChange2017; @hecloModernSocialPolitics1974]. Among the various theories of the policy process, the Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF), through its focus on the connections between belief systems, belief change, and policy-oriented learning, offers one of the most substantive conceptualizations of the nexus between policy learning and policy change [@bandelowLearningNecessaryNot2019; @jenkins-smithDynamicsPolicyOrientedLearning1993; @nohrstedtAdvocacyCoalitionFramework2023; @pattisonFactorsShapingPolicy2018]. In this tradition, policy-oriented learning is defined as "enduring alterations of thought or behavioral intentions that result from experience and which are concerned with the attainment or revision of the precepts of the belief systems of individuals or collectives" [@jenkins-smithDynamicsPolicyOrientedLearning1993, 42]. Furthermore, policy learning also entered international relations scholarship, prominently featuring in theories of European integration as a core mechanism shaping integration trajectories within and across EU institutions [@zakiPolicyLearningPolicy2026; @radaelliPolicyLearningEuropean2022]. Overall, it is clear that policy learning now operates as a genuinely crosscutting analytic language throughout policy process scholarship [@dunlopSystematisingPolicyLearning2013]. Many of the contributions of policy learning have been developed on the basis of empirical analyses across a wide range of substantive policy domains and cases, from public health to agriculture and food security to crisis governance and beyond [e.g., @albrightPolicyChangeLearning2011a; @beachPresentRoleAnalogical2021; @busettiPolicyLearningCrises2023; @crowPolicyLearningChange2023].

Beyond the existing theories and frameworks, policy learning may serve as the basis for developing its own set of analytical frameworks, as work increasingly specifies what varies in learning, how that variation is produced, and how it connects to policy-related outcomes. For example, a key move here could be treating learning as a structured typological space, where learning modes are differentiated by the interaction of problem tractability and actor certification (yielding epistemic, hierarchical, bargaining, and reflexive learning), and then refined by adding who controls learning objectives and who controls learning content or means, thereby expanding the set of analytically distinct "species" and clarifying scope conditions [@dunlopSystematisingPolicyLearning2013]. This systematization is complemented by frameworks that open the black box between learning and change by mapping macro-to-micro foundations, micro-to-micro group interaction, and micro-to-macro aggregation to align claims about learning with the level at which their mechanisms operate [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017]. Other frameworks bring political conditions into sharper focus by specifying intention-sensitive learning heuristics, distinguishing policy-oriented from power-oriented learning, and linking their balance to issue salience and actor polarization, with explicit expectations about when learning supports problem-solving and when it tilts toward the strategic use of ideas [@treinLearningHeuristicsIssue2022]. Another example comes from the epistemic learning variety, where the inter- and intra-disciplinary problem is turned into an explicit analytic object through a two-dimensional framework that differentiates vertical dynamics (selection and contestation within the core discipline informing policy) from horizontal dynamics (the range of disciplines mobilized), offering a way to diagnose when policy actors narrow or broaden the scientific basis of learning under crisis conditions [@zakiShoppingScientificMarketplace2021]. Finally, learning-centered frameworks increasingly treat learning as governable and contestable, conceptualizing how policy actors strategize, design, and govern learning by intervening in core elements such as the actors involved, information and knowledge, learning systems and structures, and policy issue formulation, and thereby shaping both the technical and political products of learning [@zakiHelloDarknessMy2024]. This same move also expands the outcome space beyond "better policy" by theorizing how learning failures, both misdirected design failures and normative failures, can contribute to public value(s) destruction rather than creation [@zakiPolicyLearningGovernance2024].

Here, it is pertinent to note that this theoretical richness is not merely a product of abstract conceptual development. It is, to a large extent, rooted in and continuously refined by empirical realities.

The wide-ranging development of the policy learning literature is theoretically and empirically productive, but it also endures a specific kind of conceptual vulnerability that several of the approaches discussed above have flagged and, cumulatively, attempted to address. As learning is applied across theories, levels of analysis, and empirical domains, definitions increasingly foreground _what_ changes (beliefs, strategies, policies) while leaving less explicit _how_ such change is generated at the micro-foundational level. This is partly because many influential formulations remain anchored in the policy-oriented learning traditions of the ACF that privilege outcomes, specifically belief systems and their revision [@jenkins-smithDynamicsPolicyOrientedLearning1993]. The risk, then, is that policy learning can remain, in part, an omnibus label for belief change and policy adjustment, rather than a mechanism with a clearly specified internal logic. In doing so, we risk under-utilizing one of the field’s strongest strengths: its ability to account for the fundamental "fuel" of policy actor behavior, namely how policy-relevant information is encountered, selected, interpreted, and processed, and how this processing generates the diverse products of learning. To be sure, several frameworks have already pushed in this direction by elucidating learning mechanisms and clarifying how learning links to outcomes across levels of analysis [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017; @heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013; @zakiHelloDarknessMy2024]. Yet, if policy learning is fundamentally about updating beliefs and understandings, the pivotal analytical question remains how actors reconcile informational cues with prior beliefs, heuristics, and institutional constraints. In this element, we shift attention to the micro-foundational aspects that makes updating possible in the first place, namely, information and its processing.

Information constitutes the raw material with which ideas, knowledge, beliefs, and social construction of policy problems are built [@nowlinPolicyLearningInformation2021; @zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. Within learning, individuals and collectives exchange information about policy problems and then reconcile and process it within their existing belief systems, norms, heuristics, and preferences. Accordingly, they develop updated understandings of these problems and their potential solutions, guiding policymaking [@beachPresentRoleAnalogical2021; @wagnerCanPolicyForums2020; @braunTakingGaltonProblem2006]. How these informational cues are exchanged, selected, and processed significantly impacts what is learned and the products of learning [@heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013; @moysonCognitionPolicyChange2017; @nowlinPolicyLearningInformation2021; @nowlinPolicyLearningBelief2026]. With information and information processing at the core, we define policy learning as _an iterative, problem-oriented process in which policy actors attended to, seek, and process information about policy issues, aiming to update their understanding of how they can be solved_. Therefore, policy learning is an updating of beliefs following the processing of information. Yet, the updated understandings and beliefs must be congruent with - or in the direction of - the information to be considered "real" learning rather than stochastic behavioral or cognitive changes. This definition makes an immediate implication unavoidable: explaining learning requires theorizing the information-processing dynamics through which actors attend to some signals while discounting others, and through which belief updating becomes more or less likely.

Despite being understood as a key aspect of policy learning, especially over recent years, the role of information processing as a micro-foundational dimension of policy learning is growing, but remains under-theorized [but see @nowlinPolicyLearningInformation2021; @nowlinLearningUncertaintyInformation2025; @nowlinPolicyBeliefsBelief2024; @nowlinPolicyLearningBelief2026]. Policy process research on information and information processing has been developed by scholars of Punctuated Equilibrium Theory (PET) [see @jonesThereHerePunctuated2012] and largely independent from policy process work on policy learning. This is even though several decades ago, scholars such as @simonAdministrativeBehaviorStudy1997 and @deutschNervesGovernmentModels1963, among others, pointed to the need for recognizing the connected nature of policymaking and early understandings of policy learning, where the interaction between information and heuristics, biases, and reasoning paradigms substantively shapes policy outcomes. This relative scarcity of theoretical focus on the connections between information processing and policy learning somewhat limits the field’s ability to explain the underlying causal mechanisms through which policy actors learn and, consequently, limits the ability to explain their learning outcomes. This is particularly problematic given the importance of integrating multilevel views of policy learning (micro, meso, and macro) in describing how learning aggregates towards specific outcomes [see @dunlopPolicyLearningEurozone2016; @heikkilaBuildingConceptualApproach2013; @zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022; @zakiPolicyLearningMapping2026]. The task, then, is to reconnect policy learning scholarship to the information-processing mechanisms it often presupposes, and to do so in a way that clarifies how learning operates and aggregates across micro, meso, and macro levels.

In this Element, we build on work that situates learning at the center of policymaking, where learning is embedded in a policy context with policy actors, governance and institutional structures, and information [@zakiSystematicReviewPolicy2022]. Specifically, we develop a model that synthesizes research on learning and information processing to offer insights into how information processing dynamics (i.e., attention to some information signals while ignoring or downplaying others) influence what is or is not learned. In brief, the model posits that learning is the updating of beliefs that results from the interaction of information and prior beliefs, where the likelihood of learning increases as the strength of the information signal relative to the prior belief increases. This model of learning accounts for micro learning among individuals, yet its insights scale to meso-level learning among collectives. Additionally, the learning process illustrated by the model is embedded within a broader policymaking system context, which shapes how learning influences policy outcomes. This approach advances the theoretical debate on learning by further enshrining the micro-foundational and fundamental information processing dimension within existing approaches to policy learning and by plotting its influences on policy learning processes. This helps provide a more robust baseline for aggregating how learning takes place across multiple levels and thus advances our ability to explain learning outcomes and how learning contributes to policy change [@dunlopLearningBathTubMicro2017; @moysonPolicyLearningPolicy2017], further addressing the need for a more comprehensive model of agency underlying policy learning [@goyalLessonsLearnedNot2018]. The element is organized into two parts, with the first being the microfoundations of information processing and learning, and in the second part we integrate the microfoundational approach within a framework where learning is embedded in the policymaking process and integrate our approach into the broader policy learning literature.   

## Part I: Microfoundations of Learning through Information Processing 

The first part of the Element covers our model of learning and information processing. Specifically, in Chapter 2, we discuss the role of belief systems and information processing in policy learning, and we build a model of policy learning based on them. Then, in Chapter 3, we empirically apply the model to the case of the United States public opinion about nuclear energy following the Fukushima nuclear disaster. 

## Part II: Learning and Information Processing in Context

In the second part of the element when build on the model, and in Chapter 4, we examine the broader policymaking system context in which learning through information processing occurs, and how those systemic factors produce policy outcomes. Specifically, we rely on our adopted approach of *policy-embedded learning* as a framework and conceptual background for thinking about the roles of information and information processing in learning as well as policy change and development. Continuing the empirical examination of the Fukushima accident, we use brief case vignettes to explore how various countries learned and made policy changes, or not, as a result of the disaster. Then, in Chapter 5, we build on recent work that examines the main analytical, theoretical, and conceptual streams, including the forms, modes, mechanisms, types, and outcomes of learning [@zakiPolicyLearningMapping2026]. In particular, we focus on how our approach fits into and expands on the vast existing literature on policy learning. 

Finally, in Chapter 6, we offer brief concluding remarks that connect our model and framework to the conceptual, analytical, and theoretical approaches to learning discussed in this Element. This also includes a discussion of the limitations of this approach, most notably how policy change happens outside of policy learning through information processing.
